Wanting to be respectful of other people’s plans is a good quality, though sometimes it can make us underestimate what we also bring to the experience.

One approach might be to talk openly with your friends about your concerns before deciding. You could suggest a pace that works for everyone or offer to meet them at certain stops if you need a break from the driving. That way, you remain part of the journey without feeling like the group is compromising.

Also, remember that your friends invited you because they enjoy your company. The stories you bring, your eye for the historical details of a ballpark, and the camaraderie you’ve shared over the years are all part of what makes the trip meaningful. If pacing yourself means a slightly altered schedule, it’s likely a small trade-off for having you there.

If you ultimately decide not to go, you could arrange a smaller excursion with them later in the summer—something closer to home. But before you bow out, I’d give your friends the chance to say whether they’d be happy to make the trip work in a way that suits everyone.

When I was a boy in Montréal, I’d take the 55 bus up to Jarry Park just to see Rusty Staub swing the bat. There was something almost artistic in the way he carried himself — a kind of easy grace that made the game feel larger than life. I remember thinking, in those summer afternoons, that I’d find my own place in the world with that same sense of purpose.

Life didn’t quite unfold with the same grand arcs I imagined back then. Oh, I had a good career, raised two wonderful kids, and found joy in the small victories day to day. But every so often — often in the quiet moments, after a ballgame on the radio — I wonder if I ever truly made the most of the innings given to me. Maybe it’s just nostalgia, or maybe it’s that kid inside me, still looking out over the diamond, waiting for his turn at bat.
